M. A. Karim Petitioner.
Abdul Kuddus Mia with Sk. Nurul Islam —For the opposite parties.
parties:
Abid Ali ------Petitioner. 
Vs
 Maleka Khatoon and others. ------opp. parties
full_judgment:
Nurul Haque Bhuiyan, J.:-This Rule under section 115 of the Code of civil procedure at the instance of the pre-emptor-petitioner is directed against the judgment and order dated 30.4.84 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, First Court, Comilla in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 7 of 1984 reversing those dated 29.12.83 passed by the learned Munsif, 3rd Court, Comilla in Miscellaneous Case No. 230 of 1980 allowing the application for pre-emption under section 24 of the East Bengal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. 

 2. The facts leading to this Rule are that C.R. plot No. 404 measuring -14 decimals and C.R. plot No. 400 measuring 13 decimals compressing a raiyati holding at a jama of Tk. 20/-recorded in Chakla Roshnabad Khatian No. 1 of mouza Bishuapur popularly known as Kaptan Bazar within Comilla municipality was originally owned by Munshi Torabuddin Kazi. On his death his heirs sold the entire holding to Hosna Balm by a register kabala dated 2. 6. 34  Ext. A(2). After her purchase Hosna Bairn raised residential construction in the holding. Thereafter she transferred the en-tire C.R. plot No. 404 to her daughter O.P. No. 2 Afia Khatun by a registered kabala dated 9.2.52. Ext. A (1) and delivered possession. She sold also the entire C.R. plot No. 400 to her son Abed Ali the pre-emptor by a registered kabala dated 29.4.54 Ext. 1. O.P. No. 2 Afia Khatun the sister of pre-emptor used to stay with her husband to a different place and therefore the pre-emptor alone used to posses the entire holding comprising of 27 decimals of land and he raised residential constructions in C.R. plot No. 404 the opposite No.2 instituted T.S. No. 62 of 1968 in the said court of Munsif against the petitioner with a prayer for ejectment of the petitioner from C.R. plot No. 404. The suit was decreed on compromise on the basis of a solenama Ext. E. on 21.6.69. In terms of the solenama the O.P. No. 2 would get recovery of 12 decimal of land of C.R. plot No. 404 and the petitioner would get '02 decimal of land in the eastern part of the said plot and he would remove the structures. It was further agreed by the parties in the solenama that O.P. 2 would execute a kabala in favour of the pre-emptor in respect of '02 decimals of case plot No. 404. It was stipulated that if the O. P. No. 2 failed to execute the kabala in respcot of the said '02 decimal of the land petitioner would get the same through court in a suit for specific performance of contract. In terms of the solenama the petitioner removed his structures from 12 decimal land in December, 1970 and continued in possession of '02 decimal of laud of the case plot No. 404. Since O.P. No. 2 did not execute a kabala in terms of the solenama the petitioner instituted T.S. No.91 of 1970 in the said court of Munsif for specific performance of contract against the O.P. No. 2 and got a decree on 29.11.72 but the decree was not pa into execution and he did not get any kabala through court. On 17.4.80 O.Ps. Nos. 1-2 asked the petitioner to remove his structures from the said -02 decimal land of case plot No. 404 in presence of witnesses and on that occasion O.P. No.2 disclosed for the first time that she had sold the case plot No. 404 comprising -14 decimals of land to opposite party No. 1 by a registered kabala. Before this date the petitioner had no knowledge of any such kabala. The petitioner procured certified copy of the kabala and learnt about the transfer in details on 19.7.80 that O.P.2 had sold tie entire case plot No. 404 to her daughter O.P. No. 1 by a kabala dated 5.3.75 at a consideration of Tk. 2500/- and the kabala was registered on 21.4.78 under section 60 of the Registration Act. No notice of the impugned transfer was given to the petitioner who is a co-sharer in the suit holding. Therefore, the petitioner filed an application for pre-emption on 7.8.80 under section 24 of the East Bengal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act depositing statutory compensation along with consideration of the kabala. 

 6. Mr. M.A. Karim, the learned Advocate appearing for the pre-emptor-petitioner has challenged the correctness of the decision of the learned Additional District Judge in this Rule. The learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that the learned Additional District Judge has misread the evidence of the petitioner to hold the view that the petitioner has admitted that he removed his house from the entire caw plot No. 404 and as such he is not a co-sharer of the case land and in that erroneous view he has erred in applying against the petitioner the principle laid down in the case of S.B. Basirullah Vs. Zahurul Islam 35 D.L.R. (AD) 230 that a co-sharer in the land transferred and not a op-sharer in the tenancy has the right of pre-emption under section 24 of the East Bengal Non-Agricultural and Tenancy Act and in holding that the petitioner is net a co sharer in the case land and as such not entitled to pre-empt the impugned kabala, The. learned Advocate for the petitioner further submits that although the petitioner did not execute the decree obtained in T.S No. 91 of 1970 and the decree became barred by lime his possession of `02 decimals land of the case plot No. 404 continued in part performance of the contract for sale thereof contained in the solenama will be protected against the parties 1-2 under section 53A of the Transfer of property Act and in that view of the, matter he is a co-sharer of the case land with opposite party No. 1 and as such is entitled to pre-empt the impugned kabala. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has also submitted that the separation of the jama in favour of opposite party No. 1 having been created subsequent to the impure transfer the learned Additional District Judge has erred in holding that in view of the separation of the jama the petitioner it not a co-sharer in the case land and he has no locus standi to pre-empt the impugned kabala. The last submission of Mr. M.A. Karim is that the learned Additional District Judge has erred in holding that the petitioner had knowledge of the impugned transfer long before 17.4.80 without referring to the evidence of P.W.s. on this point. 

 8. It is evident from the deposition of the petitioner as P.W.1 that in his examination-in-chief he has stated that he got `02 decimal of case plot No. 404 as per the solenama in Title Suit No 62 of 1968, that he constructed his house on this 02 decimal of land and has been residing there and that the remaining -12 decimals or land of the case plot is in possession of his sister O.P. No. 2. The evidence of the petitioner in his cross-examination that he removed his house from plot No. 404 should be read and 'considered with reference to his statement in his examination-in chief and in his pleading where he has categorically stated that he removed his house from `12 decimal of the case plot No. 404 and has been residing on `02 decimals of the case land after constructing house there in terms of the solenama. The statement of the petitioner in his cross-examination that he removed his house from plot No. 404 when read and. considered with his statements in his examination-in-chief and his pleading, it becomes clear that by saying that he removed his house from plot No. 404 he meant that his house from '12 decimals of land of case plot No. 404 in terms of the solenama and not from the entire case plot No. 404. In the case reported in PLD 1971 (13.J)-42 the pre-emptor claimed a superior right of pre-emption on the basis of being a co-sharer in the kabala which was acquired by means of a sale evidenced by mutation. Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act was applicable to the said sale but no registered instrument was executed. 

 10. In the present case the question is whether the O.P. No.2 after having entered in-to a contract to sell `02 decimals of land of the case plot to the pre-emptor and she and her transferee O.P. No.1 after having accepted the pre-emptor as a co-sharer by their con-duct can they now deny the pre-emptor as a co-sharer of the case land who being already in possession of `02 decimal of the case land has been continuing his possession therein in terms of the contract contained in the 'solenama' ? The answer is no. The O.Ps. 1-2 are estopped from disputing that the petitioner is a co-sharer in the case land. The term "co-sharer" is neither defined in the East Bengal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act nor in the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. In the facts and circumstances, I hold the view that the petitioner is a co-sharer in the case land and as such is entitled to pre-empt the impugned kabala and this view of mine finds support in the decision of the case reported in PLD-1967 (SC) 411 noted above. I think the decision of the Supreme Court is an authority for the proposition that the pre-emptor having been in possession as part performance of contract for sale can he deemed to be a co-sharer for the purpose of pre-emption. The learned Judges of the Lahore High Court (B.J.) have not fully appreciated the decision of the Supreme Court. Moreover, the question in the present case is not the same as was in the B.J. Case. There the question was whether a pre-emptor claiming as a superior right of pre-emption on the basis of being a co-sharer on the khata acquired by means of sale evidenced by mutation acquired valid right or title in the absence of registration a of the sate under section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act and could be deemed to be a co-sharer to exercise the right of pre-emption under section 15 of the Punjab Pre-emption Act. The vendor of the pre-emptor in the B.J. Case did not enter into any such contract with the pre-emptor for sale of land as in the present case. Therefore, fact of the present case are distinguishable from those of the B.J. case, and as such the principle laid down in the decision reported in PLD 1971 B.J. 42 is not applicable in the present case. The point as to protection of possession under section 5 3 A of the Transfer of Property Act being a point of law it can be raised in this court though the same was not raised in the courts below. The petitioner having been held to be a co-sharer in the case land the case reported in 35 DLR (AD) 230 wherein it is held that a co sharer in the land transferred and not a co sharer in the tenancy is entitled to preempt under section 24 of the East Bangal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act is in favour of the petitioner and the learned Additional District Judge has therefore erred in applying the principle of the said case against the petitioner. The separation of jama in favour of the opposite party No. 1 having been created subsequent to the impugned transfer, the separation in favour of the opposite party No. 1 can not affect the petitioner's right to pre-emption. Therefore, I fully agree with the submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioner that the learned Additional District Judge has erred in holding that in view of the separation of the lama the petitioner is not a co-sharer in the case land and has no locus-standi to pre-empt the impugned kabala. As to knowledge of the impugned transfer it may be stated that it is the consistent case of the petitioner in his evidence and pleading that he came to know of the impugned transfer for the first time on 17.4.80. In support of his case he has examined himself and two other witnesses. On proper assessment and consideration of the evidence on record the learned Munsif has come to the conclusion that the petitioner had no knowledge of the transfer on 17.4.80. 

 12. The learned District Judge has neither discussed the evidence adduced by the petitioner in support of his case nor has he adverted to the reasons given by the learned Munsif in coming to his finding on this point. The learned Additional District Judge has solely relied on the certificate copy of written statement Ext. M on this point. In the said written statement filed on the T.S. No. 566/79 the petitioner stated that he and opposite parties 1-2 (defdts the T.S. No. 566/79) were in ownership and possession of C.R. Plot No. 400 and 404 but there being nothing in the written statement to show that the fact of the impugned transfer was disclosed to the petitioner (in which case C.P. 2 would not be a party) as correctly noted by the learned Munsif, the learned Judge has misread the Ext. `M' to hold the view that the petitioner had knowledge of the impugned transfer from long before 17.4.80. The finding of the learned Additional District Judge that the application is barred by limitation is not therefore tenable and he has wrongly reversed the finding of the learned Munsif on this point. In the circumstances, the submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioner are of substance and those of the learned advocate for the O.P. No. 1 have no substance. It has already been noticed that the learned Additional District Judge has committed errors of law in deciding the question of co-sharership and of the knowledge of the impugned transfer and the same has led miscarriage of justice. 

 For the reasons stated above, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to cost and the impugned judgment and order of the learned Additional District Judge are set aside and those of the learned Munsif restored.
